blocks.text: A 52-year-old man notices that his stools have turned the colour of putty and his urine the colour of strong tea, and his skin and sclerae are yellow. Nothing is wrong with his red cells; something is stopping bilirubin from reaching the gut. Following one pigment molecule from a dying red cell to the toilet explains every one of these signs.

blocks.markdown:
**Why the liver makes bile.** Bile has two jobs: it carries away waste that the kidney cannot handle (chiefly bilirubin and cholesterol) and it supplies **bile salts**, the detergents that make dietary fat absorbable. Hepatocytes secrete bile into the **bile canaliculi**, tiny channels between adjacent cells. Canaliculi drain into bile ductules, then the hepatic ducts and the common bile duct, with the gallbladder concentrating bile between meals. Bile flow of roughly 500-600 mL/day has a bile-salt-dependent component (osmotic water follows secreted salts) and a bile-salt-independent component.

This unit follows two molecules that are recycled differently: **bilirubin**, a waste product that is mostly excreted, and **bile salts**, a functional product that is mostly saved.

blocks.title: Bilirubin and bile salts
blocks.text: Bilirubin is the orange-yellow end product of haem breakdown. Bile salts are conjugated bile acids (cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid joined to glycine or taurine) synthesised from cholesterol; they are amphipathic and form micelles above a critical concentration. Jaundice (icterus) is yellow discolouration of skin and sclerae caused by raised plasma bilirubin, usually visible once total bilirubin exceeds roughly 40-50 micromol/L (reference total bilirubin is about 5-20 micromol/L; ranges vary by laboratory).

blocks.markdown:
**Making bilirubin.** About 80% of the roughly 250-400 mg produced each day comes from haemoglobin in senescent red cells (lifespan about 120 days), engulfed by macrophages of the spleen, liver and marrow. The rest comes from ineffective erythropoiesis and from other haem proteins such as myoglobin and cytochromes.

1. **Haem oxygenase** opens the haem ring, releasing iron (recycled) and carbon monoxide and producing **biliverdin** (green).
2. **Biliverdin reductase** reduces biliverdin to **unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin**, which is lipid-soluble and poorly soluble in water.
3. In plasma, unconjugated bilirubin travels **bound to albumin**. Bound to albumin it is not filtered by the glomerulus, so it never appears in urine.
4. At the sinusoidal membrane the hepatocyte takes it up and binds it to cytoplasmic proteins.
5. **Conjugation:** UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum attaches glucuronic acid, mainly two molecules, to give **conjugated (direct) bilirubin**, which is water-soluble.
6. Conjugated bilirubin is actively secreted across the canalicular membrane (via an ATP-dependent transporter, MRP2). This is the rate-limiting step of the whole pathway.

blocks.caption: Laboratories usually report total and direct bilirubin; the indirect fraction is obtained by subtraction.

blocks.title: Which fraction is raised?
blocks.prompt: A patient has total bilirubin 62 micromol/L and direct (conjugated) bilirubin 6 micromol/L. What percentage of the total is unconjugated, and which pattern of jaundice does this suggest?

steps.text: Find the indirect fraction by subtraction.
Express as a percentage of the total.

Interpret: almost all the excess is unconjugated bilirubin. Unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and not filtered, so urine bilirubin would be absent. Conjugation or uptake is overwhelmed or impaired, so the likely patterns are excess production (haemolysis) or impaired conjugation.

blocks.answer: About 90% is unconjugated, suggesting pre-hepatic (excess production or impaired conjugation) jaundice with no bilirubin in the urine.

blocks.markdown: **What happens in the gut.** Conjugated bilirubin enters the duodenum in bile. In the terminal ileum and colon, bacteria remove the glucuronide and reduce bilirubin to **urobilinogen** (colourless). Most urobilinogen is further oxidised to **stercobilin**, which gives faeces their brown colour. Roughly 10-20% of urobilinogen is reabsorbed into portal blood; the liver re-excretes most of it into bile (a small enterohepatic loop for the pigment), and a small amount escapes to the systemic circulation and is filtered by the kidney, appearing in urine as urobilinogen and urobilin (the source of normal urine colour).

blocks.caption: Pattern of laboratory findings in the three types of jaundice (typical findings; individual cases vary).

blocks.markdown:
**Bile salts and their circulation.** Hepatocytes convert cholesterol into the **primary bile acids**, cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid. The rate-limiting enzyme is cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase. Conjugation with glycine or taurine lowers their pKa and makes them fully ionised at intestinal pH, so they stay in the lumen. Colonic bacteria dehydroxylate some to **secondary bile acids** (deoxycholic and lithocholic acid).

The **enterohepatic circulation** is the recycling loop: bile salts are secreted into bile, released into the duodenum with meals, and used to emulsify and solubilise fat. About 95% is reabsorbed, mostly by an apical sodium-dependent transporter in the **terminal ileum**, returns via the portal vein, is taken up by hepatocytes (NTCP, a sodium-dependent transporter) and re-secreted. The total pool of about 2-4 g cycles several times a day, and only about 0.2-0.6 g/day is lost in faeces, replaced by new synthesis. Returning bile salts exert negative feedback on 7-alpha-hydroxylase, so synthesis rises when reabsorption falls.

blocks.title: Daily bile salt loss
blocks.prompt: A healthy adult has a bile salt pool of 2.4 g that circulates 8 times per day. Each pass, 95% of the bile salts presented to the ileum is reabsorbed. Assuming the pool is constant, how much must the liver synthesise per day?

steps.text: Total bile salt passing through the gut per day equals pool size multiplied by number of cycles.
The fraction lost each pass is 100% - 95% = 5%.
A constant pool means synthesis must equal faecal loss, because the liver replaces exactly what is lost.

blocks.answer: About 0.96 g/day of new bile salts must be synthesised to keep the pool constant.

items: Red cell phagocytosed by macrophage; haem released from haemoglobin.
Haem oxygenase makes biliverdin; biliverdin reductase makes unconjugated bilirubin.
Unconjugated bilirubin travels on albumin to the liver (not filtered by the kidney).
UGT1A1 conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid in hepatocytes.
Conjugated bilirubin is secreted into bile canaliculi (rate-limiting step).
Gut bacteria convert it to urobilinogen; most becomes stercobilin in faeces.
A minority of urobilinogen is reabsorbed; a trace is excreted as urobilinogen/urobilin in urine.

blocks.title: Reading jaundice from the urine and stool
blocks.text: Ask where the block is. Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and reaches urine; unconjugated is not. If bile cannot reach the gut, stercobilin is missing (pale stool), urobilinogen falls, and conjugated bilirubin regurgitates into blood and urine (dark urine). If the problem is only too much unconjugated bilirubin, urine bilirubin is absent and urobilinogen is increased.

blocks.title: Bile salts and bilirubin are recycled differently
blocks.text: Do not describe bilirubin as having an efficient enterohepatic circulation. About 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed and reused, whereas conjugated bilirubin is not reabsorbed intact; it is converted to urobilinogen and mostly excreted as stercobilin, with only a small urobilinogen fraction recycled.

points: Bilirubin arises from haem breakdown (haem oxygenase then biliverdin reductase), travels on albumin, is conjugated by UGT1A1 and secreted into bile.
Gut bacteria convert conjugated bilirubin to urobilinogen and stercobilin; a small urobilinogen fraction is reabsorbed and a trace reaches urine.
Bile salts are made from cholesterol, conjugated, and recycled about 95% each pass through the ileum and portal blood, with loss replaced by synthesis.
Jaundice is classified as pre-hepatic (unconjugated), hepatic (mixed) or post-hepatic (conjugated, pale stools, dark urine) using bilirubin fractions, urine findings and liver enzymes.

questions.stem: Which enzyme converts unconjugated bilirubin into its water-soluble conjugated form in the hepatocyte?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it attaches glucuronic acid to bilirubin.
distractorRationale.b: Haem oxygenase opens the haem ring to form biliverdin, upstream of bilirubin.
distractorRationale.c: Biliverdin reductase makes bilirubin from biliverdin; it does not conjugate it.
distractorRationale.d: This is the rate-limiting enzyme of bile acid synthesis, not bilirubin conjugation.

questions.explanation: Conjugation attaches glucuronic acid to bilirubin through UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, converting a lipid-soluble pigment into a water-soluble one that can be secreted into bile. Haem oxygenase and biliverdin reductase act earlier, in macrophages, to produce bilirubin.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman has progressive jaundice, itching, pale stools and dark urine. Alkaline phosphatase is markedly raised and ALT is only mildly raised. Which urine finding is most expected?

options.text: Bilirubin present and urobilinogen absent or reduced
Bilirubin present and urobilinogen markedly increased

questions.correctOptionText: Bilirubin present and urobilinogen absent or reduced

distractorRationale.a: Correct: conjugated bilirubin regurgitates and is filtered, while no bile reaches the gut to form urobilinogen.
distractorRationale.b: This is the pre-hepatic (haemolytic) pattern, not obstruction.
distractorRationale.c: Urine bilirubin is present because conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and filtered.
distractorRationale.d: Urobilinogen needs bile in the gut; with obstruction it falls rather than rises.

questions.explanation: The picture is post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice: a cholestatic enzyme pattern with pale stools. Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble so it appears in urine and darkens it, while absent bile in the gut means little urobilinogen is formed, so urine urobilinogen is low or absent.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has Crohn disease affecting the terminal ileum and has become unable to reabsorb bile salts normally. Which change would be expected?

options.text: Increased hepatic bile acid synthesis with a reduced circulating bile salt pool
Reduced hepatic bile acid synthesis because the liver is overloaded
An enlarged bile salt pool and improved fat absorption
Increased reabsorption of bile salts in the colon, restoring the pool fully

questions.correctOptionText: Increased hepatic bile acid synthesis with a reduced circulating bile salt pool

distractorRationale.a: Correct: less return to the liver removes negative feedback, synthesis rises but cannot fully compensate, so the pool shrinks.
distractorRationale.b: Reduced return lifts feedback inhibition of 7-alpha-hydroxylase, so synthesis increases.
distractorRationale.c: Less recycling makes the pool smaller and fat absorption worse.
distractorRationale.d: The colon does not provide efficient active bile salt reabsorption.

questions.explanation: The terminal ileum is the main site of active bile salt reabsorption. When it fails, more bile salt is lost in faeces, negative feedback on 7-alpha-hydroxylase falls and synthesis increases, yet the pool is usually smaller and fat solubilisation falls.

questions.stem: Which statement about urobilinogen is correct?

options.text: It is formed from conjugated bilirubin by gut bacteria and a small fraction is reabsorbed into portal blood
It is formed from haem by haem oxygenase in macrophages
It is bound to albumin in plasma and not excreted in urine
It is the conjugated form made in the hepatocyte by glucuronic acid

questions.correctOptionText: It is formed from conjugated bilirubin by gut bacteria and a small fraction is reabsorbed into portal blood

distractorRationale.b: Haem oxygenase produces biliverdin, not urobilinogen.
distractorRationale.c: Unconjugated bilirubin, not urobilinogen, is the albumin-bound species.
distractorRationale.d: Glucuronidation produces conjugated bilirubin, which is the substrate for bacterial conversion.

questions.explanation: Gut bacteria remove the glucuronide from conjugated bilirubin and reduce it to colourless urobilinogen. Most becomes stercobilin in faeces, while a minority is reabsorbed to portal blood and mostly re-excreted by the liver, with traces reaching the urine.

questions.stem: In haemolytic (pre-hepatic) jaundice, bilirubin is characteristically found in the urine.
questions.explanation: The excess bilirubin in haemolysis is unconjugated and bound to albumin, so it is not filtered by the glomerulus and urine bilirubin is absent (acholuric jaundice). Urine urobilinogen is instead increased because more bilirubin reaches the gut.

questions.stem: A patient has a bile salt pool of 3.0 g that circulates 4 times per day. After ileal resection, only 70% of the bile salt entering the ileum is reabsorbed on each pass (previously 95%). Assuming the pool size is unchanged, what is the new daily faecal bile salt loss, in g/day?
questions.explanation: Bile salt passing through the gut per day is 3.0 g x 4 = 12 g. With 70% reabsorbed, 30% is lost each pass, so loss = 0.30 x 12 = 3.6 g/day, compared with only 0.6 g/day when 95% was reabsorbed. A loss of this size usually exceeds what hepatic synthesis can replace, so the pool shrinks and fat absorption suffers.

questions.stem: A patient has total serum bilirubin 96 micromol/L and conjugated (direct) bilirubin 8 micromol/L. Taking unconjugated bilirubin as total minus direct, what percentage of total bilirubin is unconjugated?
questions.explanation: Unconjugated bilirubin is 96 - 8 = 88 micromol/L, which is 88/96 x 100 = 91.7% of the total. A predominantly unconjugated picture points towards pre-hepatic causes (haemolysis) or impaired conjugation rather than obstruction.

questions.stem: Trace the fate of bilirubin from the breakdown of haemoglobin in a senescent red cell to its excretion, naming the enzymes and the physical form of bilirubin at each stage.
markingGuide: Senescent red cells are phagocytosed by macrophages (spleen, liver, marrow) and haem is released from globin
Haem oxygenase converts haem to biliverdin, releasing iron and carbon monoxide
Biliverdin reductase converts biliverdin to unconjugated bilirubin
Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and carried bound to albumin; it is not filtered by the kidney
Hepatocyte uptake, then conjugation with glucuronic acid by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase to give water-soluble conjugated bilirubin
Active secretion into bile canaliculi (rate-limiting step)
Gut bacteria form urobilinogen; most is oxidised to stercobilin and excreted in faeces; a small fraction is reabsorbed and a trace reaches urine
questions.explanation: Bilirubin metabolism proceeds in four phases: production, transport, conjugation and excretion. Each step changes solubility and destination, which is why the pattern of bilirubin in blood, urine and stool can localise a lesion.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman with a stone obstructing the common bile duct has deep jaundice, dark urine, pale stools and generalised itching. Explain the mechanism of each of these four features.
markingGuide: Obstruction prevents conjugated bilirubin and bile salts reaching the duodenum; back-pressure causes regurgitation into the blood
Jaundice: raised conjugated bilirubin in plasma deposits in skin and sclerae
Dark urine: conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and not albumin-bound so it is filtered and appears in urine
Pale stools: no bilirubin reaches the gut, so no urobilinogen or stercobilin is formed
Itching: retained bile salts (and other cholestatic substances) accumulate in plasma and skin
Urine urobilinogen is reduced or absent; alkaline phosphatase and GGT rise
questions.explanation: Every feature follows from bile being unable to enter the gut. The retained conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble, so it colours the urine, while the missing gut pigment explains pale stools and absent urobilinogen.

questions.stem: Describe the enterohepatic circulation of bile salts, including the site and mechanism of reabsorption, the route back to the liver, how the pool is maintained, and one consequence of its failure.
markingGuide: Bile salts are synthesised from cholesterol (7-alpha-hydroxylase rate-limiting), conjugated with glycine or taurine, and secreted into bile
Released into the duodenum, they emulsify fat and form micelles
About 95% is reabsorbed, mainly by sodium-dependent active transport in the terminal ileum
Return via the portal vein to hepatocytes (sodium-dependent uptake) and re-secretion; pool of 2-4 g cycles several times daily
Faecal loss (about 0.2-0.6 g/day) is replaced by new synthesis; returning bile salts feed back negatively on 7-alpha-hydroxylase
Failure (for example terminal ileal disease or resection) causes bile salt loss, reduced micelle formation and fat malabsorption (steatorrhoea)
questions.explanation: Recycling lets a small pool do the work of a much larger one, with the liver only replacing what is lost. When the ileal step fails, the pool falls below the critical micellar concentration after meals and fat absorption drops.
